text:
Weighting later targets mainly reweights prefix–target training examples; it does not directly favor recent conditioning items within each prefix. This follows mathematically from weighted BCE: L=Σ₍u,t₎mᵤₜwᵤₜℓᵤₜ/Σ₍u,t₎mᵤₜwᵤₜ, where m masks padding and ℓ includes positive and negative BCE. A reproducible intervention is wᵤₜ=exp[−λ(Tᵤ−t)], λ≥0, with Tᵤ the final valid target position. It emphasizes later, usually longer prefixes; any increased reliance on nearby items is indirect and requires measurement. [Original SASRec](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.09781) already learns dataset-dependent recency under ordinary shifted BCE and compares against FMC/FPMC, but does not establish the proposed weighting mechanism.

Related evidence: [Recency-based Sampling of Sequences](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643) samples targets using f(k)=α^(n−k), p(k)=f(k)/Σⱼf(j), 0<α≤1. It reports improved SASRec effectiveness and training efficiency. However, RSS removes sampled targets and changes the reconstruction task; its gains are not evidence for simply weighting shifted BCE. For direct conditioning recency, an ALiBi-style intervention uses Aₜⱼ=exp(zₜⱼ−β(t−j))/Σₖ≤ₜ,valid exp(zₜₖ−β(t−k)), β≥0, masking padding/future keys. This explicitly favors nearby keys. [ALiBi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409) supports this mechanism experimentally in language modeling, not these Amazon categories.

Useful controls: FMC score(i,j)=aᵢᵀbⱼ using only the last item, or a proposed count baseline P(j|i)=[Cᵢⱼ+γp(j)]/[ΣₖCᵢₖ+γ], with training-only adjacent counts, normalized training popularity p, and γ>0. No located study directly compares all three interventions under matched shifted BCE. Compare them on unchanged validation candidates; use recent-item versus older-item ablations to test reliance, since attention weights alone cannot establish it.
